definition: to send out a programme on television or radio
example: The final match will be broadcast live to more than a hundred countries.

definition: the title of a newspaper story, printed in large letters
example: A dramatic headline can persuade readers to buy a paper even when the story itself is weak.

definition: a newspaper with small pages that focuses on sensational stories and celebrities
example: The tabloid ran a front-page story about the singer's divorce for a week.

definition: a large-format newspaper that gives serious and detailed coverage of news
example: Readers of the broadsheet expect long analysis rather than short stories about celebrities.

definition: the work of collecting and writing news for the media
example: Investigative journalism has exposed corruption that official inquiries had failed to find.

definition: a journalist who reports on a particular subject or from a foreign place
example: The foreign correspondent sent daily reports from the capital throughout the crisis.

definition: a newspaper article in which the editors give their opinion on a topic
example: The newspaper's editorial criticised the plan as expensive and poorly thought through.

definition: a journalist who writes a regular article on a particular subject
example: The columnist argued that television news has become too focused on entertainment.

definition: the number of copies of a newspaper or magazine sold
example: Printed newspapers have seen their circulation fall as readers turn to online news.

definition: the total number of people who read a particular publication
example: The magazine has a young readership, with most readers aged between eighteen and thirty.

definition: an arrangement to pay in advance to receive a publication or service regularly
example: An annual subscription to the magazine costs less than buying each issue separately.

definition: the right of newspapers and journalists to report without government control
example: Press freedom is essential for a democracy because it allows citizens to question their leaders.

definition: the control of what the public may see or read, often by a government
example: Censorship of the news makes it hard for ordinary people to know what is really happening.

definition: designed to shock or excite the public, often by exaggerating
example: Sensationalist reporting can create public panic about risks that are in fact very small.

definition: an unfair preference for one side that affects how information is presented
example: Viewers should be aware of bias when a channel is owned by a political party.

definition: treating all sides fairly and not favouring any of them
example: Public broadcasters are expected to give impartial coverage of every election.

definition: the quality of being based on facts rather than personal feelings
example: Complete objectivity is difficult because journalists choose which facts to include.

definition: the quality of being trusted and believed
example: A newspaper loses credibility if it publishes a story before checking the facts.

definition: false or inaccurate information that is spread, whether deliberately or not
example: Misinformation about vaccines spread rapidly through online groups during the outbreak.

definition: false information that is spread deliberately to deceive people
example: A foreign disinformation campaign tried to influence the outcome of the vote.

definition: false stories that appear to be real news, often spread online
example: Many teenagers say they cannot tell the difference between fake news and genuine reports.

definition: information used to promote a political cause or point of view, often misleading
example: During the war, posters and radio broadcasts were used as propaganda to raise morale.

definition: exaggerated publicity intended to attract public attention
example: The film failed to live up to the hype that surrounded its release.

definition: online content designed to attract attention and encourage people to click a link
example: Clickbait headlines promise a surprise but usually deliver very little real information.

definition: public support for a product by a famous person
example: A celebrity endorsement can double sales of a sports drink within months.

definition: the particular group of people at whom a product or programme is aimed
example: Advertisers research their target audience carefully before choosing which channel to use.

definition: the hours in the evening when the largest number of people watch television
example: Advertising during prime time is far more expensive than during the afternoon.

definition: a film or programme that presents real events and facts
example: The documentary followed three refugee families for five years.

definition: a television drama series about the daily lives of a group of characters
example: My grandmother has watched the same soap opera every evening for thirty years.

definition: a television programme that follows real people in unscripted situations
example: Critics say that every reality show rewards conflict because it increases ratings.

definition: political and social events that are happening now
example: Young people who follow current affairs tend to be more active in local politics.

definition: a short broadcast report of the latest news
example: The radio station broadcasts a news bulletin at the start of every hour.

definition: reports on an event that are broadcast as it happens
example: Live coverage of the election results kept viewers awake until dawn.

definition: the amount and kind of attention that an issue receives from news organisations
example: Heavy media coverage of the trial turned the defendant into a household name.

definition: an important news story that one newspaper gets before its rivals
example: The reporter got a scoop when she obtained the minister's private letter.

definition: a news report that reveals something shocking or hidden
example: A newspaper exposé revealed that the company had been dumping waste in the river.

definition: photographers who follow famous people to take pictures of them
example: The actress said that the paparazzi followed her everywhere, even to her children's school.

definition: a famous person, especially in entertainment or sport
example: Celebrity culture encourages young people to value fame more than hard work.

definition: casual talk about other people's private lives, often not true
example: Magazines full of gossip about film stars sell well at supermarket checkouts.

definition: disturbing a person's private life in an unwelcome way
example: Intrusive reporting about the family's grief caused widespread public anger.

definition: the act of disturbing a person's private life without their permission
collocations: feel like an invasion of privacy
example: Publishing the couple's private photographs was ruled an invasion of privacy by the court.

definition: the publication of false statements that damage a person's reputation
example: The newspaper paid damages after the businessman successfully sued for libel.

definition: the act of harming someone's reputation by making false statements
example: The politician launched a defamation case against the magazine that accused him of bribery.

definition: a survey that asks a sample of people what they think about a topic
example: The latest opinion poll shows that most voters distrust the national press.

definition: spreading very quickly and widely through the internet
example: The clip went viral within hours and was watched by millions of people.

definition: currently popular and being discussed a great deal online
example: A trending hashtag can turn a local protest into a national story overnight.

definition: a person who affects what others buy or do through their online following
example: Brands pay an influencer to recommend products to a large number of followers.

definition: a person who subscribes to someone's online account to see their posts
example: She gained a million followers after sharing a video about her cooking.

definition: to watch many episodes of a television series one after another
example: On rainy weekends my friends and I like to binge-watch a whole season of a drama.

definition: a person who spends a lot of time sitting watching television
example: If children spend six hours a day on screens, they risk turning into couch potatoes.

definition: accepting what happens without taking action
example: Television makes viewers passive, because they simply receive what is shown.

definition: to make someone less able to feel strong emotions about something
example: Constant exposure to violent images may desensitise young viewers to real suffering.

definition: to show something in a picture, film or piece of writing
example: The documentary depicts daily life in a remote fishing village with great sensitivity.

definition: to make something seem more attractive or exciting than it really is
example: Some music videos glamorise an expensive lifestyle that most viewers can never afford.

definition: to control or influence people or information in a clever, unfair way
example: Governments can manipulate the news to hide their failures from the public.

definition: to influence someone's opinion or decision
example: Emotional stories can sway readers more than statistics and expert arguments.

definition: giving a lot of useful facts or ideas
example: The museum's website is informative and easy to navigate.

definition: so exciting or interesting that it holds your attention
example: I found the new thriller so gripping that I read it in one night.

definition: extremely interesting and holding your complete attention
example: Her speech was riveting, and nobody in the hall looked at a phone.

definition: so interesting or convincing that people cannot ignore it
example: The article offers a compelling argument for reducing the amount of advertising aimed at children.

definition: accepted by most people and typical of the majority
example: Ideas that were once on the margins have been taken up by mainstream newspapers.

definition: appealing to a small specialised group of people
example: Podcasts on specialist hobbies attract a small but loyal niche audience.

definition: a newspaper, channel or website through which information is communicated
example: A single owner now controls several leading media outlets in the country.

definition: a very powerful and wealthy owner of newspapers and television companies
example: The media mogul used his newspapers to support the party that promised him lower taxes.

definition: an official statement given to journalists by an organisation
example: The company issued a press release to deny the rumours of an imminent takeover.

definition: a long piece in a newspaper or magazine that covers a subject in depth
example: The magazine's feature article about the housing crisis was shared more than any other story that year.

definition: translated words shown at the bottom of the screen during a film
example: Subtitles let people watch foreign films without losing the original actors' voices.

definition: figures that show how many people watch or listen to a programme
example: Falling ratings led the broadcaster to cancel the show after only one series.

definition: an exciting ending that leaves the audience wanting to know what happens next
example: Each episode ended with a cliffhanger, which made it almost impossible to stop watching.

definition: spoken comments in a film or advert by someone who is not seen on screen
example: The famous naturalist provided the voiceover for the wildlife series.

definition: an advertisement on television or radio
example: The commercial for the new phone was shown during every break in the football match.

definition: a person or company that pays to promote products in the media
example: Newspapers depend on advertisers, which can make editors cautious about criticising them.

definition: a person who reads the news on television or radio
example: The newsreader apologised on air for reading an incorrect headline.

definition: a system that stops people reading a website's content unless they pay
example: Many online newspapers have introduced a paywall because advertising income alone is no longer enough.

definition: presenting news in a way intended to shock or excite rather than inform
example: Sensationalism in crime reporting can make the public overestimate the risk of violence.
